newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamist PM faces opposition wrath.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamist PM faces opposition wrath.

text.p: The secularist opposition on Wednesday hammered Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan for turning Turkey away from the West and toward the Moslem world, but appeared unable to muster the votes to bring him down.

Speaking ahead of a bid to hold a censure motion that could topple Erbakan's coalition, MPs accused Erbakan of bringing Turkey into disrepute during a recent visit to Libya, where he was lectured about Turkey's treatment of its minority Kurds.
The visit also provoked a rare public rebuke by NATO ally Washington, long Turkey's foremost foreign ally but now wary of its first Islamist leader in the modern era.
"The junior coalition partner is fond of the West, the other partner (Erbakan) cannot take his heart and eyes off the dictatorial regimes of the East," said leftist MP Ismail Cem.
Deniz Baykal, a former foreign minister, said Erbakan had abandoned responsibilities at home for adventures abroad.
"The new government rushed to a state which has a proven, close relation to terrorism...this was a mistake," he said of Erbakan, who was not in the hall as the debate opened.
His remarks touched off tit-for-tat charges between government and opposition MPs, delaying a vote on the censure motion to allow the right to reply.
Despite the public pasting, Erbakan and coalition partner Tansu Ciller remained confident ahead of the vote.
"As long as the coalition protocol exists the government will continue," Ciller told MPs from her True Path Party (DYP) before the debate.
A look at the numbers supports the government's case.
Senior Ciller aides said they were confident they could hold their 120 deputies when a motion to hold a confidence vote came to the floor. One DYP deputy resigned just before the debate.
For its part Welfare, whose iron discipline effectively bars dissent, boasts 160 MPs. That gives the ruling coalition a margin of four seats beyond the 276 needed to guarantee victory.

Despite this cushion, the government was braced for a rough ride from opposition MPs, frustrated by increasing gridlock and angered by Erbakan's attempts to refashion Turkey's traditional westward orientation.
"It's clear the opposition's...attack will not be enough to topple Erbakan," political analyst Derya Sazak wrote in daily Milliyet. He predicted a rough ride for the premier.
"Today's parliamentary session will be worth watching. It is the opposition's day."

Erbakan's "eastern policy" blew up in his face 10 days ago when Libyan leader Muammer Gaddafi used an Erbakan visit as a platform to blast NATO member Turkey's ties to the West and its treatment of the Kurds.

Erbakan's stunned silence in the face of these remarks, as well as his own anti-Western rhetoric while in Libya, provoked condemnation at home and a broadside from the United States, which accuses Libya of support for terrorism.

Closer to home, inflation is running at 80 percent, and many bankers and other analysts expect it to burst into triple digits. Huge budget deficits have fed sky-high interest rates, robbing the economy of funds needed for investment.

The Turkish lira has been sinking against the dollar each day. And foreign investors, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund have all warned of dire consequences if the government does not take matters in hand.
On Tuesday, a confident Erbakan assured his party faithful the government would emerge unscathed, and even strenghtened, from its first test since taking power on June 28.
"This vote will strengthen the government further. The government will be a lot stronger, it will continue on its way," the veteran Welfare leader said. "We will serve until the year 2000," he vowed.
